Revised after review. Rashi (after Menachem; he notes another reading omits this), Meiri and both Metzudot read בַּלַּע as 'destroy, undo'; Radak says 'destroy them so that their counsel is confounded'. 'Confuse' is STEPBible's gloss (a Piel of בלע) and I keep it in the glosses, but the commentaries do not support it as their reading. I also dropped the earlier claim that the KJV's 'Destroy' flattens the verb: it follows the commentators, and the 'confusion' sense is carried by the next verb, פַּלַּג. Whether the verb is 'swallow' (YLT) or 'confound' is a real split among the five English versions; I chose 'swallow up' in the literal layer to keep the Hebrew root visible.

agent_notes: The subject is a single 'he' after the plural 'them' of vv.16 and 20; the commentators (Rashi, Radak, Meiri, Malbim) identify him as Ahithophel, an identification the psalm itself does not make. I did not name him in the translations.

Machma'ot is a hapax; KJV and Rashi read 'butter/curds' (chem'ah). The pointing machma'ot with an a-vowel in the mem has led many to emend to mehem'ot or 'than curds' (mi-chem'ah) giving 'smoother than butter'. YLT's 'sweeter than honey' follows a different tradition. I keep 'creamy things' in the literal layer. Pitchot: 'drawn swords' (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat Zion citing Mic 5:5), against Rashi's alternative reading as an Aramaic curse-writ.

Yehav is a hapax, 'what has been given you' (Ibn Ezra, citing a view that it comes from yahav 'give'), the KJV 'burden' follows the Talmudic rendering (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat Zion). I give both in the literal layer and the note.

The dramatic layer now says 'will not live out half their days' (Metzudat David: 'will not reach half of their days'; Ibn Ezra: their number of days will not be filled). Ibn Ezra offers a second reading of the last clause, 'I trust you to fill my days'; I keep 'I trust in you' without an object clause.

agent_notes: אָרִיד and וְאָהִימָה are rare. Rashi and Ibn Ezra tie אָרִיד to a root meaning 'to be restless, to wander' (Lam 3:19, Judg 11:37); Menachem takes it as 'rule', which I did not follow. I read אָהִימָה as 'I moan, I am in uproar' (hum, cf. 'tumult'). The five English versions split between 'mourn', 'am restless' and 'am made low'.
